home.about.002: My starting point is electrical and electronic engineering. My next questions lie in robotics, control, and the intelligence we can put close to a machine.
home.about.003: I’m completing a BEng (Hons) at the University of Nottingham Ningbo China, with graduation expected in July 2027. I’m preparing for postgraduate study across embedded systems, control and automation, cyber-physical systems, and edge AI.
home.about.004: My current final-year project is a simulation-based study of digital-delay compensation and prediction robustness in PMSM predictive torque control. The work is exploratory; hardware validation remains ahead.
home.about.005: Across these projects, I care about what can be measured, what can be explained, and where a person should retain control.
home.about.006: <1>Explorer of words & worlds.</1> Outside engineering, I enjoy reading, learning languages and travelling.
home.about.007: I’m also looking for internships in embedded systems, robotics, control, electronics testing, and applied AI. During term, I can discuss 2–3 on-site visits per week near UNNC, with hours arranged around classes.

doppler-radar.007: The analogue front end amplifies and filters the radar output before ADC sampling. The STM32 estimates frequency using FFT processing, converts it to speed and sends formatted digits to the CPLD display. The integrated demonstration uses a 5 kHz sampling rate; the separate FFT exercise uses 10 kHz.

forward-converter.003: Within Group 07, I worked on converter and compensation design, PLECS modelling, winding and characterising magnetic components, and investigating regulation and switching spikes.
forward-converter.004: The team report documents the team system; the role summary above follows my recorded project contribution.
forward-converter.006: The design targets a 10 V, 5 A output. The report compares ideal and non-ideal PLECS models, transformer and inductor design, and Type I and Type III compensation. Magnetic components were characterised with an LCR bridge before open-loop and closed-loop measurements.
forward-converter.007: The power-stage diagram above shows the converter topology; it is not the full compensation circuit. The report uses the Venable K-factor method for the Type III compensator.
forward-converter.009: Under the report’s heavy-load AC test, Type I compensation shows a 100 Hz ripple envelope of 1.092 V. The Type III example reports 10.02 V output and 84 mV ripple. The two oscilloscope captures use different time scales: they illustrate the reported low-frequency behaviour and should not be treated as a direct comparison of switching spikes.

bangbang-v2.overview.001: Bangbang is a collaborative tele-operated avatar-robot platform. Facial-expression and bilingual speech cues support an operator who can inspect the interaction and choose how to respond.
bangbang-v2.overview.002: The project produced two distinct conference papers: a perception study (HRFEST Paper 230) and an operator-assistance study (IHCI Paper 99). The submitted FURP 2026 poster brings these strands together.
bangbang-v2.overview.003: My work focused on the facial-perception pipeline and its Raspberry Pi 5 integration: a shared MediaPipe facial-landmark front end, a learned CNN/ONNX route and an interpretable action-unit route.
bangbang-v2.overview.004: The wider team contributed speech, operator-interface and teleoperation components. The perception outputs describe visible movement; they are not validated measurements of internal emotion or a clinical condition.

bangbang-v2.results.003: The Paper 99 presentation shows local and cloud AI assistance, bilingual input and a browser interface for reviewing suggested replies. Chinese speech recognition uses a cloud service. Its timing figures are development observations with varying prompts and settings; they do not form a controlled model ranking.
bangbang-v2.results.004: Functional checks and demonstrations show particular prototype functions. They do not establish end-to-end reliability, accurate interpretation of emotion, reduced operator workload or user benefit. Those questions need further evaluation.

pi-engineering-assistant.005: Base + Tools; 54 of 96 answers met the study’s fully-correct criterion.
pi-engineering-assistant.007: Closed-book Base only. This is a different configuration, not a matched hardware comparison with Base + Tools.
pi-engineering-assistant.overview.001: A compact language model can give a fluent answer while using the wrong material or making an arithmetic error. This prototype pairs a four-bit Qwen3-1.7B model with course-material retrieval and deterministic calculation tools.
pi-engineering-assistant.overview.002: <1>Ask</1> shows an answer alongside its sources or calculation trace. <2>Quiz</2> reveals feedback and supporting sources after an answer is submitted. The platform targets a Raspberry Pi 5; the reported evaluation separates its components and devices.
pi-engineering-assistant.overview.003: I led implementation of the edge prototype, integrated retrieval and calculation tools, built the inspectable Ask/Quiz workflow, and compared system configurations within the team project.
pi-engineering-assistant.alt.001: Raspberry Pi 5 hardware and the Ask and Quiz workflows
pi-engineering-assistant.results.001: The main evaluation compared seven configurations on 96 EEE questions using an offline GPU reference. The table reports mean rubric scores on a 0–1 scale and the number of answers meeting the study’s fully-correct criterion.
pi-engineering-assistant.results.013: RAG means retrieval-augmented generation; SFT means supervised fine-tuning. Rubric scores are not accuracy percentages. Base + Tools is the tool-augmented RAG configuration: supported calculations use the deterministic Calculator; other requests use retrieval. The highlighted GPU Base + Tools and Pi closed-book Base results test different configurations and must not be read as a matched hardware comparison.
pi-engineering-assistant.results.014: A separate matched closed-book Base comparison used the same quantised model artefact and 96 questions on both devices: GPU mean 0.503; Pi mean 0.498. The mean difference (Pi − GPU) was −0.005, with a 95% interval from −0.041 to +0.032. The study did not establish equal answer quality.
pi-engineering-assistant.results.015: On a separate 24-question retrieval-sensitive set, Base+RAG scored 0.779 versus 0.325 for closed-book Base (a +0.454 mean change). The Holm-adjusted test for fully-correct outcomes was p = 0.0625, which did not meet the 0.05 threshold. On 24 pre-classified calculator-supported questions, Base+Tools scored +1.000 mean over Base+RAG. Neither tested SFT recipe exceeded its matched Base configuration.
pi-engineering-assistant.results.016: The evaluation used AI-assisted rubric scoring followed by author review, not independent blinded validation. Device observations and selected web demonstrations are separate evidence layers. The study did not test learning benefits, usability or end-to-end web reliability. A displayed source or trace helps inspection but does not itself establish that an answer is correct.

pi-engineering-assistant.record.005: Generic language-model assistants do not naturally align with a particular course. We present a Raspberry Pi 5-targeted platform combining a compact Qwen3-1.7B model, course-grounded retrieval, deterministic calculation, and a Web portal that exposes answers, evidence, and tool execution. It is configurable for individual course requirements; we evaluate system quality and edge deployment, not learning outcomes. GPU-accelerated evaluation compares seven configurations over 96 course questions: closed-book generation, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), Calculator execution, and two supervised fine-tuning (SFT) recipes. A separate 24-question set compares Base and Base+RAG approaches. Base + Tool-Augmented RAG achieved the highest mean rubric score of 0.777 on a 0–1 scale. Retrieval improved mean source-sensitive quality; deterministic Calculator execution gave the clearest gain on 24 preclassified supported items. Neither SFT recipe demonstrated improvement over its matched Base configuration. A paired 96-question Base comparison did not detect a directional GPU–Pi score difference; the Pi ran the same quantized artifact more slowly.

robot-elevator-interaction.record.003: Existing robot-accessible elevator interfaces require manufacturer-specific retrofits which are costly and difficult to scale. Direct physical interaction with existing elevator panels offers a promising infrastructure-independent alternative, but requires robots to reliably perceive, interpret, and actuate controls despite variations in panel layouts, lighting conditions, reflections, and labeling conventions. We present an edge-based prototype system with an end-to-end perception-to-action pipeline that integrates task-specific button detection, specialized target recognition, vision-language semantic understanding, confidence-aware rejection, semantic-state maintenance, asynchronous processing, and physical button actuation. We evaluate perception performance, static-image target selection, runtime behaviour, and physical actuation through two qualitative button-activation demonstrations. Across 475 target-selection requests derived from 112 static RGB images spanning six buildings, the system selected the intended button in 404 cases, achieving an accuracy of 85.1%. On a separate benchmark of 379 human-annotated Open/Close/Other button crops, the HOG+SVM classifier achieved a macro-F1 score of 0.9963. During a 207-s runtime evaluation, the system filtered 99.8% of redundant candidate-level semantic requests, with no observed label switching, flicker, crashes, or camera interruptions. In both operator-initiated physical button-activation demonstrations, the robotic arm activated the selected button, withdrew, and returned to its standby state. These results provide practical insights and design considerations for the development of robust, edge-based, offline, and real-time robot–elevator interaction systems.
